title: Neighborhood social infrastructure is unevenly available and connected to belonging and mutual aid
source_unit: Survey Center on American Life American Neighbor Survey, Ipsos KnowledgePanel probability-based panel

denominator.unit: US adults age 18 and older in the qualified weighted survey sample

regular_neighbor_conversation.unit: percent talking with neighbors at least a few times a week

worked_with_neighbors.unit: percent working with neighborhood residents in the prior 12 months to fix a problem or improve the community

neighbor_trust.unit: percent reporting a great or fair amount of trust that neighborhood residents do the right thing

neighbor_trust_high_school_or_less.unit: percent among adults with a high school degree or less

third_places_none.unit: percent reporting no listed neighborhood amenity within a 20-minute walk

third_places_six_or_more.unit: percent reporting six or more listed neighborhood amenities within a 20-minute walk

weekly_neighbor_conversation_no_third_pl.unit: percent among adults reporting no listed neighborhood amenities

weekly_neighbor_conversation_six_or_more.unit: percent among adults reporting six or more listed neighborhood amenities

comfortable_neighbor_childcare_college_p.unit: percent of parents with a college degree comfortable asking a neighbor to watch a child in an emergency

comfortable_neighbor_childcare_noncolleg.unit: percent of parents without a college degree

observations.method: Weighted descriptive estimates from a probability-based online panel recruited through address-based sampling; interviews were conducted in English and Spanish, with weighting for gender, race and ethnicity, education, region, income, language dominance, race by age, race by education, and 2024 presidential vote.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is cross-sectional and relies on self-reports and stated comfort or trust. The third-place, education, housing, age, and religious-attendance comparisons are associations; the source does not establish that amenities, education, homeownership, or religion causes interaction, trust, or mutual aid. The 2012 comparison is an aggregate survey comparison, not a recontact panel.
observations.subgroup: Education, age, housing tenure/type, religious attendance, and neighborhood-amenity categories as reported by the source; the source reports a qualified-sample margin of sampling error of plus or minus 1.55 percentage points and design effect 1.35.
observations.counterinterpretation: People with stronger resources, longer residence, different life stages, or greater willingness to walk may both select into better-connected places and report more neighborhood interaction; observed amenity gradients may therefore reflect selection, mobility, safety, or unmeasured place conditions rather than a direct third-place effect.

related_sources.claim: Pew provides a complementary local-trust and stated mutual-aid layer using a different survey and question set.
Census HTOPS provides a current household social-connectedness route but is a separate survey design and should not be pooled with this panel.

boundary: This record describes neighborhood interaction, trust, amenities, stated mutual aid, and belonging-related preferences. It does not observe a dated shock, actual assistance delivered, time or money transferred, adequacy, formal-service interaction, recovery, later political action, or a causal effect of social infrastructure.
